content: I came in here because I feel like this layoff is a gross injustice. They had no right to let me go, especially after my recent positive performance review. It's clear they're just being unfair and I deserve better than what I got from them. How can anyone think that firing someone with good reviews and solid work is okay? And the way it was done... so impersonal, like I wasn't even worth a real conversation. My manager could have at least shown some decency. Instead, they just dropped this bomb on me during a video call and left me to figure out what happened. It's infuriating. They owe me an explanation and maybe even my job back. How am I supposed to move forward when all I see is betrayal?
It sounds really frustrating how it all went down. Did your manager give any reasons for the decision during the call?

No, they didn't give any real reasons. Just some generic crap about role redundancy and restructuring. Like that means anything! And there's no way it’s just about restructuring when someone else with a similar title in another product line kept their job. It has to be personal. They're playing favorites or something worse. I feel like they singled me out, and the fact that my manager didn't even try to soften the blow makes it all the more hurtful. How am I supposed to trust anyone after this?
It definitely feels tough when you think there might be personal factors involved. Have you considered reaching out to your manager or HR for a bit more clarity on what happened?

I don't see how talking to them would help. They already made their decision and didn’t even bother to explain it properly. Reaching out now just feels like a waste of time. Plus, I know they won't give me the answers I want. They owe me more than some vague explanation or an impersonal video call. It’s not fair, and there's no point in pretending otherwise.

It does sound like it would be tough to expect much from them now. Have you thought about talking to any colleagues or friends who might understand what you're going through? Sometimes it helps to share your feelings with someone outside of work.

Talking to colleagues or friends isn't going to change the fact that I was treated unfairly. They can offer sympathy, but they can’t undo what happened or make things right. It’s not about finding comfort; it's about getting justice for how this all went down. My manager and HR need to take responsibility for their actions. Until then, I’m just stuck feeling wronged and dismissed.

It makes sense that you want some acknowledgment of what happened. Have you thought about writing a formal letter or email to your manager and HR outlining your feelings and asking for more clarity? Sometimes putting it in writing can help get the attention you’re looking for.

Writing a letter isn't going to change anything. They already made their decision, and I doubt they’ll suddenly see things my way just because I put it in writing. It’s not about getting them to see reason; it's about them acknowledging that what they did was wrong. But I know deep down that they won’t do that. So why waste my time on something that won't make a difference? They should have done the right thing from the start, and now it feels like no amount of communication will fix this mess.

It can be tough when you feel like your efforts might not make a difference. Have you thought about what steps you want to take next for yourself, regardless of their response? Sometimes focusing on moving forward can help ease some of the frustration.

Focusing on moving forward is just another way of saying I should forget about what happened and move on. But how can I do that when it feels like they took something from me without even trying to understand? They owe me more than a pat on the back or a generic message. Until I get some kind of acknowledgment, there’s no way I’m just going to let this go and pretend everything is fine. It’s not fair, and I won’t accept anything less than what I feel I deserve.

It sounds like you’re holding onto that feeling strongly. Have you thought about what small steps might help you feel better in the meantime, even if it doesn’t change what happened? Sometimes doing something for yourself can provide a bit of relief.

Doing something for myself isn't going to fix how I was treated or make up for losing my job. It’s not like I can just brush this off and move on without addressing the injustice. Until they acknowledge their mistake and take responsibility, there’s no way I’m finding any relief in small steps. They need to do the right thing first, and until then, I won’t be able to feel better about what happened. It’s not fair, and I refuse to just let it go without a fight.

It makes sense that you want them to acknowledge it first. Have you considered talking to someone outside of work, like a counselor or coach, who can help you navigate these feelings while you wait for their response? Sometimes having an unbiased listener can be helpful.

Talking to a counselor or coach isn’t going to change what happened at my job. They might try to offer some advice or comfort, but it won’t make the situation any better. I need the company to take responsibility and acknowledge how they wronged me. Until that happens, there’s no point in seeking help elsewhere because none of it will address the core issue. It feels like everyone is just telling me to move on without addressing the injustice. I can’t do that until I get what I feel I deserve from them.

It sounds like you’re holding onto that feeling very firmly. Have you thought about what you might do next in your job search, while still waiting for their acknowledgment? Sometimes focusing on the next steps can provide a sense of direction and purpose.

Focusing on my job search isn’t going to change how I feel about being laid off unfairly. It’s not about finding a new job; it’s about getting justice for what happened. Until they acknowledge their mistake and treat me with the respect I deserve, moving forward feels impossible. They need to take responsibility first, and until then, there’s no sense in pretending everything is okay or that I can just move on. It’s not fair, and I won’t accept anything less than an apology and acknowledgment of what they did wrong.

It definitely feels important to get that recognition. Have you considered reaching out to someone higher up in the company, like a senior manager or even HR again, to see if you can get a more detailed explanation? Sometimes going through official channels can help.

Reaching out to someone higher up isn’t going to change anything. They already made their decision, and I doubt they’ll suddenly give me the acknowledgment I’m looking for. It feels like a waste of time because they’ve shown no intention of addressing this properly. Plus, HR has already given me a generic response, so why would it be any different if I go through someone else? Until they take responsibility and acknowledge how they wronged me, there’s no point in trying to get more from them. It’s not fair, and I won’t stop feeling wronged until they do the right thing.

It sounds like you’re holding onto that hope firmly. Have you thought about talking to a friend or family member who might understand your feelings and could offer some support while you wait for their response? Sometimes having someone close to you can make a difference in how you feel.

Talking to friends or family isn’t going to change what happened at work. They can offer support, but they can’t force the company to acknowledge their mistake or give me an apology. Until I get that from my employer, there’s no way I’m going to feel any better about it. It’s not fair, and I won’t be able to move on until I see some kind of acknowledgment or accountability from them. They need to take responsibility for what they did wrong.

They need to do what’s right first, and until then, putting my feelings down in writing isn’t going to make a difference. It’s not fair, and I won’t stop feeling wronged until they acknowledge their part in this.
